explainer.heading: Heat always flows from hot to cold
explainer.body: Heat moves from a hotter object to a colder one until both reach the same temperature.
explainer.example: A hot cup of chai cools down on the table because heat flows into the cooler air around it.
explainer.hook: Heat is a traveller that always goes downhill: hot ➜ cold.

explainer.heading: Conduction
explainer.body: In solids, heat passes from particle to particle without the particles moving from their place. Metals are good conductors; wood, plastic and air are poor conductors (insulators).
explainer.example: A steel spoon in hot dal gets hot at the handle; a wooden ladle doesn't.

explainer.heading: Convection
explainer.body: In liquids and gases, warmer parts become lighter and rise while cooler parts sink, setting up currents that carry heat.
explainer.example: Sea breeze: by day land heats faster, warm air over land rises and cooler air from the sea moves in.

explainer.heading: Radiation
explainer.body: Heat can travel as waves without any medium, even through empty space. Dark surfaces absorb more radiant heat; light surfaces reflect more.
explainer.example: We feel the Sun's warmth though space between us is empty. White clothes keep you cooler in summer.

questions.q: Which mode of heat transfer does not need any medium?
questions.why: Radiation travels as waves, even through empty space.

questions.q: Heat moves in solids mainly by:
questions.why: Particles in solids pass heat to neighbours without moving.

questions.q: Wood is a good conductor of heat.
questions.why: Wood is a poor conductor (an insulator), which is why cooking spoons often have wooden handles.

questions.q: During the day, a sea breeze blows from:
questions.why: Land heats faster; warm air over land rises and cooler sea air moves in.

questions.q: In a pot of water heated from below, hot water rises and cold water sinks. This is called ______.
questions.why: Convection currents carry heat in liquids and gases.

questions.q: Why are we advised to wear light-coloured clothes in summer?
questions.why: Light colours reflect radiant heat; dark colours absorb it.

questions.q: Which of these is the best insulator?
questions.why: Air is a poor conductor; trapped air in woollens and double windows keeps heat in.

questions.q: Heat flows from a colder object to a hotter object.
questions.why: Heat always flows from hotter to colder.

questions.q: Woollen clothes keep us warm in winter mainly because:
options: Wool traps air, a poor conductor
questions.ans: Wool traps air, a poor conductor
questions.why: Trapped air slows the flow of body heat to the surroundings.

questions.q: Explain the land breeze that blows at night near the coast.
questions.ans: At night land cools faster than the sea; air over the warmer sea rises and cooler air from land moves towards the sea.
questions.why: Reverse of the sea breeze, driven by convection.

questions.q: Ice is kept in a box lined with thermocol. Thermocol helps because it is:
questions.why: It slows heat from outside reaching the ice.

questions.q: Why are ventilators placed near the ceiling of a room?
questions.ans: Warm air is lighter and rises; ventilators near the ceiling let warm air escape while cooler fresh air enters from below.
